slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by framing the appendix as a structural cleanup of Euclidean motion. The learner already knows translations, rotations, and reflections geometrically; the goal here is to make their common algebraic shape visible. Emphasize that the source span is short but powerful because it turns distance preservation into the affine formula used throughout differential geometry.

slides.title: Route
slides.notes: Use this as the map for the session, not as a list to rush through. The lecture repeatedly returns to the same computational object, an affine map with a matrix and a vector. Students should hear that the diagrams are inspections of one theorem from several angles: distance, orientation, fixed points, and composition.

slides.title: Definition
slides.notes: The definition is intentionally pairwise: no privileged origin, axis, or parameterization is mentioned. This is why a translation can be an isometry even though every coordinate changes. Point to the ledger idea and ask students what would fail first if one vertex were stretched away from the others.

slides.title: Normal Form
slides.notes: State the theorem as the central fact of the appendix. The important pedagogical move is to separate the two jobs: the matrix controls the frame, and the vector controls the location. When students later meet surface isometries, this Euclidean result should feel like the flat model sitting in the background.

slides.title: Distance Ledger
slides.notes: This slide connects the theorem to a reproducible finite test from the notebook. The residual values are not the proof, but they train the right eye: all pairwise distances move together. Explain that numerical darkness in the heat map means the whole constellation has been moved rigidly, not individually adjusted.

slides.title: Translations
slides.notes: Translations are the easiest case to underestimate, because nothing appears to rotate or reflect. Stress that the affine formula needs them: without the vector a, every isometry would be forced to fix the origin. The diagram should be read as a vector field whose uniformity rules out shear, scaling, and rotation about a point.

slides.title: Orthogonal Matrices
slides.notes: This is the algebraic hinge of the theorem. Rather than treating orthogonality as a matrix slogan, walk through the inner product computation and let length preservation fall out as a special case. The message is that an orthogonal matrix is exactly a rigid change of frame at the origin.

slides.title: Orientation
slides.notes: The determinant is a compact orientation ledger. In the plane it can be read through signed area; in three dimensions it becomes handedness of ordered triples. Make clear that direct and opposite describe orientation behavior, not whether the motion is visually dramatic or small.

slides.title: Reflection Formula
slides.notes: Treat the formula as a geometric sentence. The scalar v dot N minus d measures signed distance to the mirror, and multiplying by N turns it into a normal vector. Subtracting twice that vector moves the point to the opposite side while leaving all points of the hyperplane fixed.

slides.title: Fixed Sets
slides.notes: Fixed sets are a useful diagnostic because they translate algebra into geometry. The equation F(v)=v becomes a linear system once F(v)=Pv+a is known. Invite students to compare how much of the space remains still: none, one point, a line, a plane, or an axis depending on the motion.

slides.title: Rotations
slides.notes: This slide makes the columns of a rotation matrix tangible. Each column is where a basis vector lands, so orthogonality says the image basis remains perpendicular and unit length. The determinant being one adds the orientation information: the ordered basis still has the same handedness.

slides.title: Two Reflections
slides.notes: The determinant signs already predict that two reflections should be direct, since negative times negative is positive. The geometry sharpens that prediction into a rotation angle. Use the diagram to follow one vector through the intermediate reflected position and then to the final rotated position.

slides.title: Composition
slides.notes: Composition is where the affine viewpoint earns its keep. Students often remember the QP part but forget that the translation a is rotated or reflected by Q before b is added. Tie this to doing one rigid motion and then measuring the next one in the moved coordinate frame.

slides.title: 3D Orientation
slides.notes: The three dimensional version of orientation is handedness. The cross-product identity is a compact way to see that direct motions preserve the right-hand rule while opposite motions reverse it. Mention that the notebook includes an interactive scene, but this slide distills the invariant being checked.

slides.title: Classify
slides.notes: This is the applied lab translated into lecture form. The point is not to memorize a taxonomy first; the point is to ask a stable sequence of questions that exposes the taxonomy. Students should see that determinant sign, distance residual, and fixed-set dimension are complementary pieces of evidence.

slides.title: Common Mistakes
slides.notes: Use this slide as a checkpoint before the summary. Each mistake corresponds to a specific algebraic omission: the translation vector, determinant sign, normal direction, composition rule, or orthogonality condition. A good way to run the slide is to ask which invariant would catch each error.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the formula and asking students to name what each term controls. The appendix is valuable because it compresses familiar rigid motions into a reusable algebraic language. The next time an isometry appears, the first reflex should be to look for the orthogonal matrix, the translation vector, determinant sign, and fixed-set equation.
